name: Sabaic
world_status: statement found in an open source

earlier_scan.source_named: Beeston, A.F.L. 1984. Sabaic Grammar (JSS Monograph 6). Epigraphic language; stress likely unrecoverable from consonantal script; grammar not found online

new_statements.quote: Apart from these few hints, practically nothing is known about the vocalization of the Ancient South Arabian texts preserved for us. The question of a possible differentiation of syllables according to vowel quantity, therefore, likewise cannot be answered with certainty, nor are any broad conclusions possible concerning the accentual relationships of Ancient South Arabian.
new_statements.citation: Nebes, Norbert & Peter Stein. 2008. Ancient South Arabian. In Roger D. Woodard (ed.), The Ancient Languages of Syria-Palestine and Arabia, 145-178. Cambridge: Cambridge University Press.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No rule: the language is attested only in a consonantal script with no oral tradition, so vowel quantity, syllable structure and accent cannot be recovered; the authoritative modern sketch states explicitly that no conclusions about accent are possible.
new_statements.exceptions: None. Kogan & Korotayev 1997: 224 speculate only that the Minaic 'parasitic' h reflects 'a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch)', without locating stress.
new_statements.domain_note: Applies to Ancient South Arabian as a whole (Sabaic, Minaic, Qatabanic, Hadramitic), with Sabaic the base of the description; epigraphic texts only, no citation forms exist.
new_statements.identity_note: Sabaic is an extinct epigraphic language (c. 8th c. BCE - 6th c. CE) known only from a purely consonantal script. The deciding source describes Ancient South Arabian as a whole with Sabaic as its base; the Kogan & Korotayev 1997 remark on stress concerns Minaic (mina1268 family area; Glottolog Minaic) rather than Sabaic specifically. Sister Glottolog codes held under source_audit: mina1267/1268/1269, hadr1235/1236, saba1265/1267/1268/1276.

sources.note: p. 223: 'Since the South Arabian system of writing is purely consonantal, we cannot draw any direct information about Sayhadic vowels'; p. 224 on Minaic 'parasitic' h: 'Though it remains uncertain under what conditions this appears, it is thought that it was caused by a peculiar character of the stress (possibly even pitch).' No stress-placement rule.
